Athanasius the Great

Icons

Saints

St. Athanasius the Great

St. Athanasius of Alexandria

What is depictedHistory and traditionPublished explanationSources

St. Athanasius the Great of Alexandria is the saint identified in this medieval Constantinopolitan mosaic. This is distinct from St. Athanasius the Athonite. The pictured historical artwork and the theological author’s text are separately sourced.

[1] Exact artwork file: Description, Creator, Date, Credit and licence fields; complete downloaded image visually compared

What is depicted

The image shows the upper half of Saint Athanasius in episcopal vestments in the diakonikon of the parekklesion at the Pammakaristos church, now Fethiye Camii, Istanbul. Dumbarton Oaks supplies the photograph under CC0. Its 1949–1963 photographic dating is not the mosaic’s medieval creation date.

[1] Exact artwork file: Description, Creator, Date, Credit and licence fields; complete downloaded image visually compared

History and tradition

The institutional record names the architectural location and depicted saint. It is a historical wall mosaic, reproduced from the Dumbarton Oaks photographic collection, rather than a modern painted portrait. The separate image credit preserves the institution’s specific release and the original object’s identity.

[1] Exact artwork file: Description, Creator, Date, Credit and licence fields; complete downloaded image visually compared

Published explanation

For He was made man that we might be made God [347] ; and He manifested Himself by a body that we might receive the idea of the unseen Father; and He endured the insolence of men that we might inherit immortality.

[2] On the Incarnation, section 54, paragraph 3, first complete sentence

4. And, in a word, the achievements of the Saviour, resulting from His becoming man, are of such kind and number, that if one should wish to enumerate them, he may be compared to men who gaze at the expanse of the sea and wish to count its waves. For as one cannot take in the whole of the waves with his eyes, for those which are coming on baffle the sense of him that attempts it; so for him that would take in all the achievements of Christ in the body, it is impossible to take in the whole, even by reckoning them up, as those which go beyond his thought are more than those he thinks he has taken in.

[2] On the Incarnation, section 54, paragraph 4
